title: The God who sees me (Genesis 16)
hook: Hagar, a runaway slave, is found by God at a spring and names him the God who sees

segments.voice: Yesterday, amen: an old man under a crowded sky, leaning on a promise. Your line: so shall your seed be.

Ten years in the land, and still no child. So Sarai makes a plan: she gives her Egyptian slave, Hagar, to Abram, so that a child born to Hagar would count as Sarai's. The story never gives Hagar a say in any of it. She becomes pregnant, and then everything goes wrong. Hagar looks down on Sarai. Sarai blames Abram. Abram says, she's your slave, do what you like. Sarai treats her harshly, and Hagar runs. A pregnant woman, alone, heading into the desert toward Egypt, toward home. Nobody in the household goes after her. But someone does.
screen: `TEN YEARS, STILL NO CHILD.` → `HAGAR HAS NO SAY.` → `SHE RUNS INTO THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: By a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur, the angel of the LORD finds her: an Egyptian slave girl on the run. And he does something nobody in the story has done. He calls her by name. In the King James Bible: "Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?" Where have you come from, where are you going: the questions you ask a person, not property. She answers honestly: I'm running away. What he says next is hard. He tells her to go back and submit to Sarai. It's a hard line, and the text doesn't explain it. But he also gives her a promise like Abram's: descendants too many to count. And a name for her son: Ishmael, which means God hears, "because the LORD hath heard thy affliction." Then Hagar does something remarkable. She names God. "And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me." In Hebrew, El Roi, the God who sees me. An enslaved foreign woman with no power at all gives God a name. And the well there was called Beer-lahai-roi, the text says, because of what she said. Christians, and the Jews and Muslims who also remember Hagar, have found in this scene something steady. The person the household didn't see, the story says, God saw.
screen: `THE ANGEL FINDS HER AT A SPRING.` · `HE CALLS HER BY NAME.` · `ISHMAEL: GOD HEARS.` · `SHE NAMES GOD.` · then, large: `THOU GOD SEEST ME.`

segments.voice: Think about someone around you who's easy not to see, the person who cleans the office after hours, the new kid, the relative everyone talks over, and picture their face: do you know their name, where they've come from, where they're going? If you pray, you can pray for them by name, or by the name you don't know yet. If you don't, just hold their face in mind for a while.
El Roi. The God who sees me. The name Hagar, a runaway slave, gives to God at a spring in the desert.
Your line: you are seen. The one nobody went after was found. Day three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray to God as El Roi, the God who sees, especially in seasons of loneliness or mistreatment, and Hagar's story is often told in ministries that serve women, migrants and people in hardship.

notes: 'The first time the Bible mentions the angel of the LORD' (16:7). Confirm.
'One of the very few people in the whole Bible who gives God a name': often said to be the only one; softened. Confirm.
The command to return and submit (16:9) is acknowledged as hard and left unexplained. Confirm the handling is acceptable.
Neighbor mention: Jews and Muslims also remember Hagar (Hajar in Islamic tradition). Brief and unranked; confirm.
Beer-lahai-roi glossed 'the well of the Living One who sees me'; the meaning of the name is debated by translators; confirm.

Reviewer fix: 'Hagar has no say' softened to 'the story never gives Hagar a say' (the text is silent rather than stating it); practice given a line for those who don't pray; neighbor sentence smoothed. Also note: the previous day's carry, 'so shall your seed be', modernizes KJV 'So shall thy seed be' (15:5); it is a carry line, left unchanged here.
